title: Data-free Multistep Diffusion Distillation

paper.title: Data-free Multistep Diffusion Distillation
paper.abstract: Abstract One-step diffusion distillation achieves strong performance on small datasets but remains insufficient for high-resolution or complex text-to-image settings. Extending to multistep distillation often requires training data, suffers from early-step degradation, inconsistent outputs across sampling budgets, and incurs high computational cost. We identify that these limitations stem from simultaneous training, where a single adapted network approximates multiple score functions of different student distributions at once, causing biased distribution matching and unstable optimization. Therefore, we propose Progressive Multistep Data-free Distillation (PMDD), which assigns a dedicated adapted network per student distribution while avoiding the memory overhead of maintaining multiple adapted networks. Combined with a stage-wise unforget loss to preserve earlier-step generations, PMDD reduces optimization bias in the student, provides faster convergence, and a single unified model that supports multiple inference budgets. Extensive experiments show that PMDD matches or outperforms data-free few-step baselines at every multistep budget, reaches FID 1.99 on ImageNet 64 × \times 64 in two steps, below its 512-NFE teacher (2.32), and achieves FID 7.76 on zero-shot COCO 512 × \times 512, while requiring 4–5 × \times less training compute than data-free DMDv2 to support three inference budgets.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models have attained significant success in generative tasks, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in a wide range of domains such as image generation [ 41 , 42 , 12 , 39 ] , audio synthesis [ 5 , 15 ] , and text generation [ 1 , 10 , 24 ] . Diffusion-based image generation models adopt an iterative denoising process which gradually removes noise from a noisy intermediate sample to reconstruct a high-quality image. However, the sampling process is inherently slow, typically requiring hundreds or thousands of neural function evaluations (NFEs), which makes the models expensive for many real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, recent research has explored distilling a (diffusion) teacher into a (diffusion) student. These approaches fall into two families. ​ T ​ r ​ a ​ j ​ e ​ c ​ t ​ o ​ r ​ y − m ​ a ​ t ​ c ​ h ​ i ​ n ​ g \emph{Trajectory-matching} methods [ 25 , 37 , 40 , 26 , 6 , 14 ] regress the student onto the teacher’s deterministic ODE trajectory, and typically require real samples or adversarial training to match their teachers. ​ D ​ i ​ s ​ t ​ r ​ i ​ b ​ u ​ t ​ i ​ o ​ n − m ​ a ​ t ​ c ​ h ​ i ​ n ​ g \emph{Distribution-matching} methods, motivated by frameworks such as GMMNs [ 18 ] and GANs [ 8 ] , instead learn a one-step mapping x 0 | ϕ , T = g ϕ ​ ( x T , T ) x_{0|\phi,T}=g_{\phi}\left(x_{T},T\right) from Gaussian noise x T ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , ℐ ) x_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\mathcal{I}\right) to clean data, and align the ​ d ​ i ​ s ​ t ​ r ​ i ​ b ​ u ​ t ​ i ​ o ​ n \emph{distribution} of student outputs with that of the teacher. An adapted network φ \varphi is introduced to estimate the score function of the student distribution and guide it toward the teacher distribution. While effective on small- and medium-scale datasets such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 64 × 64 64\times 64 , one-step distillation struggles with complex text-image compositions and high-resolution synthesis [ 27 , 31 , 51 , 50 , 55 ] . Therefore, extending distillation to few steps is necessary to achieve higher fidelity generation while preserving most of the sampling speedup. To enable multistep sampling, prior approaches naively extend the one-step framework, allocating a single adapted network φ \varphi to simultaneously approximate N N score functions corresponding to distributions produced by g ϕ ​ ( x t i , t i ) g_{\phi}\left(x_{t_{i}},t_{i}\right) ( i = 1 , … , N i=1,...,N ) [ 53 , 50 , 38 ] . This single design choice is, we argue, the root cause of the field’s current limitations. Forcing one network to fit N N heterogeneous score targets within a shared parameter space induces ​ n ​ e ​ g ​ a ​ t ​ i ​ v ​ e ​ t ​ r ​ a ​ n ​ s ​ f ​ e ​ r \emph{negativetransfer} : the network cannot fit any single target well, yielding biased distribution matching at every timestep. Compounding this, the student’s intermediate predictions are imperfect and continuously evolving during training, the student thus optimizes against drifting, high-variance targets. Together these effects produce distribution mismatch, amplify error accumulation, and destabilize optimization. These theoretical pathologies have concrete consequences. First, increasing the number of sampling steps often yields only marginal improvement, or even degradation [ 50 , 53 ] , forcing existing methods to heavily rely on ​ 𝐫 ​ 𝐞 ​ 𝐚 ​ 𝐥 − 𝐢 ​ 𝐦 ​ 𝐚 ​ 𝐠 ​ 𝐞 \boldsymbol{\emph{real-image}} adversarial training to boost visual quality. Second, training is extremely costly: MMD runs each experiment on 256 TPU v5e chips [ 38 ] , while DMDv2 consumes 64 A100 GPUs per model [ 50 ] . Third, the simultaneous objective lacks consistency across sampling budgets: a model trained for N N -step inference produces high-quality output only at N N steps, while 1 1 to N − 1 N{-}1 steps degrade. Supporting N N budgets therefore requires training N N separate models, multiplying substantial training cost. We introduce Progressive Multistep Data-free Distillation (PMDD) , a novel framework whose central mechanism directly removes the single-shared-network bottleneck. PMDD assigns a ​ d ​ e ​ d ​ i ​ c ​ a ​ t ​ e ​ d \emph{dedicated} adapted network to each student score function g ϕ ​ ( x t i , t i ) g_{\phi}\left(x_{t_{i}},t_{i}\right) , so every stage is modeled accurately and free of negative transfer. To avoid the linear memory growth this would naively imply, PMDD adopts a ​ p ​ r ​ o ​ g ​ r ​ e ​ s ​ s ​ i ​ v ​ e \emph{progressive} schedule that incrementally transforms a K K -step student into a K + 1 K{+}1 -step student, building from 1 1 up to N N steps. Each new stage is trained on samples drawn from the ​ p ​ r ​ e ​ v ​ i ​ o ​ u ​ s ​ l ​ y ​ d ​ i ​ s ​ t ​ i ​ l ​ l ​ e ​ d \emph{previouslydistilled} student, which already approximates the relevant marginal well, replacing the drifting, high-variance targets of simultaneous training with stable ones, and sharply accelerating convergence. Finally, an ​ u ​ n ​ f ​ o ​ r ​ g ​ e ​ t ​ t ​ i ​ n ​ g ​ l ​ o ​ s ​ s \emph{unforgettingloss} regularizes against the previous student, preserving earlier-step behavior so that one PMDD model produces consistent, high-quality output across ​ a ​ l ​ l \emph{all} inference budgets, a property no prior data-free method offers. We evaluate our approach across various tasks, including conditional image generation on CIFAR-10 [ 16 ] , ImageNet 64 × \times 64 [ 36 ] , and zero-shot text-to-image generation on MS COCO 512 × \times 512 [ 19 ] . PMDD improves with the number of steps and matches or outperforms data-free few-step baselines at every multistep budget, including FS-SiD [ 53 ] , reaching FID 7.76 on MS-COCO 2014-30k, while supporting three inference budgets at 4–5 × \times lower training compute than data-free DMDv2. We further show that a single PMDD model maintains strong consistency across inference budgets, with higher step counts progressively refining detail while preserving global structure, and that the framework generalizes to higher-resolution 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 setting.

sections.text: A one-step student is often limited to model complex data distributions effectively. To overcome this limitation, multi-step diffusion distillation trains an N N -step student model g ϕ g_{\phi} to generate data samples sequentially from N N time steps t 1 t_{1} , t 2 t_{2} , …, t N t_{N} , where 0 < t N < t N − 1 < … < t 1 = T 0<t_{N}<t_{N-1}<\ldots<t_{1}=T . sections.heading: 3.1 Progressive Data-free Multi-step Distillation
sections.text: To overcome the limitations of existing multi-step distillation approaches discussed in Section 2.2 , we propose a progressive multi-step diffusion distillation framework instead of jointly learning the student mapping across all N N steps. In our approach, the student g ϕ g_{\phi} is distilled sequentially in multiple stages, progressing from 1 1 to N N . Specifically, at the first stage ( t 1 = T t_{1}=T ), we train a one-step student g ϕ 1 g^{1}_{\phi} using Gaussian noise as inputs, following the one-step distillation framework described in Section 2.1 . Suppose that after stage i − 1 i-1 , we have obtained an ( i − 1 ) (i-1) -step student g ϕ i − 1 g^{i-1}_{\phi} capable of generating clean samples from step t 1 t_{1} up to step t i − 1 t_{i-1} . At stage i i , we leverage this previously distilled student to learn g ϕ i g^{i}_{\phi} , which extends generation capability up to step t i t_{i} . This procedure is repeated progressively until the final N N -step student g ϕ N g^{N}_{\phi} is learned. sections.heading: 3.2 Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting
sections.text: Solely optimizing the student objective in Eq. 11 leads to severe catastrophic forgetting. This occurs because, as training progresses, the student increasingly concentrates on learning the t i → 0 t_{i}\rightarrow 0 mapping, while neglecting previously learned mappings from earlier steps t k t_{k} ( k < i k<i ) – which are excluded from gradient updates due to the stop-gradient operation. Consequently, using the i i -step student to generate samples in fewer steps k k ( k ≤ i k\leq i ) noticeably degrades both semantic and visual fidelity. To address this issue, we augment Eq. 11 with an unforgetting regularizer : ℒ unf stu , i ​ ( ϕ ) = ∑ k = 1 i − 1 𝔼 x T , x t k ​ [ ‖ g ϕ i ​ ( x t k , t k ) − g old k ​ ( x t k , t k ) ‖ 2 2 ] \mathcal{L}^{\text{stu},i}_{\text{unf}}\left(\phi\right)=\sum^{i-1}_{k=1}\mathbb{E}_{x_{T},x_{t_{k}}}\left[\left\|g^{i}_{\phi}\left(x_{t_{k}},t_{k}\right)-g^{k}_{\text{old}}\left(x_{t_{k}},t_{k}\right)\right\|^{2}_{2}\right] This enforces consistency between current student g ϕ i g^{i}_{\phi} and the previously distilled students at their respective time steps, thereby preserving the learned mappings t k → 0 t_{k}\rightarrow 0 for k = 1 , … , i − 1 k=1,...,i-1 . However, this formulation incurs a significant memory overhead that grows linearly with i i , because it requires retaining all i − 1 i-1 prior student models. To improve scalability, we adopt a more memory-efficient variant: ℒ unf stu , i ​ ( ϕ ) = ∑ k = 1 i − 1 𝔼 x T , x t k ​ [ ‖ g ϕ i ​ ( x t k , t k ) − g old i − 1 ​ ( x t k , t k ) ‖ 2 2 ] \mathcal{L}^{\text{stu},i}_{\text{unf}}\left(\phi\right)=\sum^{i-1}_{k=1}\mathbb{E}_{x_{T},x_{t_{k}}}\left[\left\|g^{i}_{\phi}\left(x_{t_{k}},t_{k}\right)-g^{i-1}_{\text{old}}\left(x_{t_{k}},t_{k}\right)\right\|^{2}_{2}\right] (12) This alternative leverages the most recently distilled student g old i − 1 g^{i-1}_{\text{old}} as the reference for all earlier steps, rather than storing all prior models. Since g old i − 1 g^{i-1}_{\text{old}} already maintains high-quality mappings from t 1 t_{1} , …, t i − 2 t_{i-2} to 0, a triangle-inequality bound (Appendix A.2) decomposes the deviation from every earlier student into at most N − 1 N-1 per-stage residuals, reducing memory complexity to 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) in the number of stages (Section 4.4.3 ). Overall, the student is optimized with the following loss: ℒ stu , i ​ ( ϕ ) = ℒ DM stu , i ​ ( ϕ ) + α ​ ℒ unf stu , i ​ ( ϕ ) \mathcal{L}^{\text{stu},i}\left(\phi\right)=\mathcal{L}^{\text{stu},i}_{\text{DM}}\left(\phi\right)+\text{$\alpha$}\mathcal{L}^{\text{stu},i}_{\text{unf}}\left(\phi\right)

sections.heading: 4.1 Performance Comparison
sections.text: PMDD is the strongest multistep data-free distiller in both guidance regimes (Table 1 ​ a ~\ref{fig:main_table}a ). Under low guidance, three steps reach FID 7.76 7.76 , below the 50 50 -step teacher at CFG = 3 \,=3 (8.78), the data-free DMDv2 at the same CFG (9.02), and the data-dependent FS-SiD+GAN at 4 4 steps, without real data or a GAN loss. Under high guidance, two PMDD steps match the best CLIP score of ​ f ​ o ​ u ​ r − s ​ t ​ e ​ p \emph{four-step} FS-SiD (0.319) at a lower FID (14.83 vs. 16.60). On ImageNet64 (Table 1 b), two-step PMDD surpasses its 512-NFE teacher (1.99 vs. 2.32) and data-free DMDv2. These gains extend to perceptual quality. PMDD maintains a consistent ≈ \approx 75% HPSv2 win rate over DMDv2 across diverse visual themes (Figure 3 ), and produces more photo-realistic, better prompt-aligned images (Figure 4 ). DMDv2 hallucinates implausible scenes (water unnaturally surrounding the lighthouse, first row) while the teacher omits key components (“coastline” in first row; “waterfall” in second row). PMDD avoids both failures, preserving both primary attributes and subtle context. This quality holds across step budgets with a single model, which we quantify in Section 4.2 Figure 3 : HPSv2 win rate: PMDD vs. DF-DMDv2. These results support our two core design choices: per-stage networks remove the excess score-matching error Δ i \Delta_{i} of a shared network (Proposition 1 ), and the frozen previous-step g old i − 1 g^{i-1}_{\text{old}} provides low-variance targets that stabilize optimization (Section 4.4.4 ).

sections.heading: 4.2 Flexible Inference from a single model
sections.text: A practical limitation of simultaneous distillation is that each target step count requires a separately trained model. PMDD removes this constraint: a single model serves any step budget, refining rather than recomposing. To quantify consistency, we fix the initial noise x T x_{T} and measure how much a model’s output changes as the step count varies. Table 2 reports LPIPS and SSIM between step budgets where PMDD stays more consistent than DMDv2 on every step pair. Figures 1 and 4 show this qualitatively: DMDv2’s layout shifts and degrades at low budgets, while PMDD holds its composition and sharpens detail. This stability is the direct effect of our unforgetting loss ℒ unf stu , i ​ ( ϕ ) \mathcal{L}^{\text{stu},i}_{\text{unf}}(\phi) , which preserves global structure across budgets so that extra steps refine an image rather than recompose it. sections.heading: 4.3 Training Efficiency
sections.text: At inference, PMDD deploys a single student and discards all per-stage adapted networks and unforgetting regularizer. The savings are at training time: to support N N inference budgets, simultaneous methods train N N times, paying N × N\times the cost, whereas PMDD pays once in the first stage and finetunes each later stage from the previous one (Table 4 ). Supporting three budgets on SD v1.5 thus takes 4.3 × 4.3\times fewer synthetic samples and 4.4 × 4.4\times less time than DMDv2, with each additional step costing under 3% of the first stage’s samples (convergence in Appendix C). These gains stem from our progressive design, which reuses each stage to build the next for delivering multi-budget flexibility and high training efficiency. sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: One-step distillation achieves great performance on small- and medium-sized resolution [ 31 , 54 , 45 , 55 , 51 , 49 ] building on Score Distillation Sampling [ 33 ] and Variational Score Distillation [ 46 ] . Several methods have been designed to extend distillation from one-step to multistep settings for higher resolution. However, they naively extend from the one-step distillation approach, which uses a single adapted network to learn the score function corresponding to data distributions induced by g ϕ ​ ( x t i , t i ) g_{\phi}\left(x_{t_{i}},t_{i}\right) ( i = 1 , … , N i=1,...,N ). Because these student distributions are themselves imperfect and evolve during training, the shared network must jointly model multiple unstable targets, causing distribution mismatch, error accumulation, and unstable optimization (Section 2.2 ). Therefore, quality improves only marginally with additional sampling steps and, in some cases, fails to improve. In contrast, our key novelty is to assign a distinct adapted network to each student to each stage through our progressive training mechanism. Our extensive experiment validates this design, demonstrating more training-efficient and superior performance. A separate line of work distills by ​ m ​ a ​ t ​ c ​ h ​ i ​ n ​ g ​ t ​ h ​ e ​ t ​ e ​ a ​ c ​ h ​ e ​ r ′ ​ s ​ s ​ a ​ m ​ p ​ l ​ i ​ n ​ g ​ t ​ r ​ a ​ j ​ e ​ c ​ t ​ o ​ r ​ y \emph{matchingtheteacher^{\prime}ssamplingtrajectory} , which regresses the student onto points along the teacher’s deterministic ODE trajectory. Typically, they require real data/images or teacher’s trajectories for learning [ 37 , 25 , 22 , 21 , 14 , 26 , 40 , 9 ] . PMDD differs fundamentally: it is data-free and distribution-matching, aligning student and teacher distributions through a learned score estimate without ever referencing a real sample or a teacher trajectory. This distinction is sharpest against Progressive Distillation (PD) [ 37 ] , with which our method shares a “progressive design”. PD’s progression ​ h ​ a ​ l ​ v ​ e ​ s \emph{halves} the number of sampling steps, compressing a 2 ​ k 2k -step teacher into a k k -step student, so each student is upper-bounded by its teacher and trades quality for speed. PMDD instead distills a teacher into a one-step student, then incrementally extends a k k -step student into k + 1 k+1 step one, improving quality as steps increase.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Progressive Multistep Data-free Distillation (PMDD). Simultaneous distillation fits a single adapted network to all steps at once, on inputs produced by a student that is itself changing. PMDD instead matches each stage with its own adapted network on inputs from the frozen previous student, and an unforgetting loss keeps a single model usable at every budget. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet 64 × 64 64\times 64 , COCO 512 × 512 512\times 512 and MJHQ-30K 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 , PMDD matches or outperforms data-free baselines at every multistep budget and improves with every added step on both U-Net and Transformer backbones, at 4–5 × \times lower training cost than one data-free DMDv2 model per budget. We focus on the few-step regime ( N < 4 N<4 ); beyond it, sampling approaches the teacher’s inference cost, diminishing the advantage of distillation.

sections.heading: Appendix E Extended Related Work
sections.text: In this work, we focus on distributional matching diffusion distillation, which can be broadly grouped into two categories: either one-step or multi-step. Single-step generation focuses on aligning the distributions of the student and teacher across different time steps. SwiftBrush adapts 3D distribution matching techniques from Score Distillation Sampling [ 32 ] and Variational Score Distillation [ 46 ] to 2D image synthesis by replacing the 3D NeRF rendering component with a 2D text-to-image generator. To further improve image fidelity, DMD [ 51 ] augments the framework with an additional regression loss on synthetic data, while other methods rely on adversarial objectives during distillation [ 44 , 49 ] . Score Identity Distillation [ 55 ] generalizes this idea by replacing the reverse KL-Divergence used in original work with Fisher Divergence, featuring DMD as its special case while remaining data-free. Several methods have been designed to extend distillation from one-step to multistep settings. Multistep Moment Matching [ 38 ] performs first-moment alignment and attains state-of-the-art results; however, it operates in pixel space rather than latent space, leading to substantial model size and computational overhead. DMDv2 [ 50 ] and FS-SiD [ 53 ] extend one-step distribution matching to multiple steps with a single shared adapted network; TDM [ 28 ] combines both distribution and trajectory matching approaches, and Decoupled DMD [ 20 ] improves few-step text-to-image distillation through decoupled training objectives. All retain a shared score estimator across steps; PMDD instead decouples score estimation per stage via progressive mechanism, yielding cross-step consistency and a single model for all budgets.
